lessonMetadata.title: Go CSP Concurrency & Channel Primitives
lessonMetadata.tagline: Master goroutines, buffered channels, select multiplexing, and deadlock prevention.

cyberAcademy.title: Chapter 1: Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP) in Go
cyberAcademy.tagline: Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating.
objectives: Differentiate between OS threads and M:N multiplexed goroutines
Understand unbuffered vs buffered channel synchronization semantics
Multiplex I/O channels cleanly using non-blocking select statements
Prevent goroutine leaks and synchronization deadlocks
cyberAcademy.chapterSummary: Go implements Tony Hoares Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP) paradigm. Instead of guarding shared mutable state with complex mutex locks, Go encourages passing ownership of data through typed channels.

deepDive.title: Go Runtime M:N Scheduler & Work Stealing
deepDive.content: The Go runtime schedules thousands of lightweight goroutines (G) across logical processors (P) and OS threads (M). When a goroutine blocks on a network call or channel operation, the scheduler parks G and steals work from other queues to keep CPU cores 100% saturated.

takeaways: Goroutines begin with a tiny 2KB stack that grows dynamically as needed.
Sending to an unbuffered channel blocks until a receiver is ready.
Closing a closed channel panics; always close from the sender side.
Use select with a default case to execute non-blocking channel polling.

slides.title: Goroutines & Channels: The Pipe Model
slides.content: Channels are synchronization conduits. When goroutines send and receive on an unbuffered channel, they perform an atomic handshake where data is handed off directly between memory stacks.
slides.sandboxCode:
package main
import "fmt"
func main() {
    ch := make(chan string, 1)
    ch <- "Hello from channel"
    fmt.Println(<-ch)
}

slides.title: FIFO Channel Ordering
slides.prompt: A buffered channel of capacity 2 receives 10 and then 20. What does <-ch return first?
slides.codeSnippet:
ch := make(chan int, 2)
ch <- 10
ch <- 20
fmt.Println(<-ch)

options.feedback: 🎯 Correct! Go channels strictly maintain First-In, First-Out (FIFO) queue order.
Incorrect. Channels are queues (FIFO), not stacks (LIFO).
Incorrect. Channel reads return individual elements.
Incorrect. The buffer has capacity 2, so writes do not block.

slides.title: Unbuffered Channel Self-Deadlock
slides.content: Sending to an unbuffered channel in the main goroutine without an active concurrent receiver causes an immediate fatal deadlock panic.

questions.prompt: [Lesson Drill 1] What does this buffered channel operation output?
questions.code:
package main
import "fmt"

func main() {
    ch := make(chan int, 2)
    ch <- 2
    ch <- 3
    fmt.Println(<-ch)
}
questions.explanation: Channels are FIFO queues. The first value sent is the first value received.
questions.hint: Remember channels operate in First-In, First-Out (FIFO) sequence.

questions.prompt: [Lesson Drill 1] What is printed by this select multiplexer with default case?
questions.explanation: Since the channel buffer is empty and no sender is ready, the select default case executes immediately without blocking.
questions.hint: A select statement with a default case never blocks.
